title: Do you need to install Spark on all nodes of a YARN cluster (no — Spark runs on top of YARN and uses YARN to get resources; install Spark only on the submitter/edge node)?
shortTitle: Do you need Spark installed on all nodes of a YARN cluster?
topicTitle: Do you need to install Spark on all nodes of a YARN cluster (no

s1_definition.profdef: No, you do not need Spark installed on every YARN node. Spark runs on top of YARN as an application: the client submits the job from a submitter or edge node that has Spark installed, YARN allocates containers on worker nodes, and Spark ships its own jars to those containers at launch. The worker nodes run YARN NodeManagers and the JVMs YARN starts; they do not need a pre-installed Spark. In practice you install Spark only on the edge node, and optionally stage the Spark archive in HDFS so YARN distributes it to containers.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of YARN as the National Bank's building manager who hands out empty meeting rooms (containers) on demand. Spark is a consultant who brings their own laptop and materials (the Spark jars) into whatever room they are given. You do not need to pre-stock every room with the consultant's materials — the consultant carries them in each time. You only keep the consultant's office (the edge node) fully equipped.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spark is a YARN application that ships its own jars to containers, so install Spark only on the edge/submitter node, not on every worker.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No, you do not need Spark installed on every YARN node. Spark runs on top of YARN as an application: the client submits the job from a submitter or edge node that has Spark installed, YARN allocates containers on worker nodes, and Spark ships its own jars to those containers at launch. The worker nodes run YARN NodeManagers and the JVMs YARN starts; they do not need a pre-installed Spark. In practice you install Spark only on the edge node, and optionally stage the Spark archive in HDFS so YARN distributes it to containers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of YARN as the National Bank's building manager who hands out empty meeting rooms (containers) on demand. Spark is a consultant who brings their own laptop and materials (the Spark jars) into whatever room they are given. You do not need to pre-stock every room with the consultant's materials — the consultant carries them in each time. You only keep the consultant's office (the edge node) fully equipped.

**One line to remember:** Spark is a YARN application that ships its own jars to containers, so install Spark only on the edge/submitter node, not on every worker.

sections.s2_technical:
YARN is Hadoop's resource manager. It has a ResourceManager that schedules and NodeManagers on each worker that launch and monitor containers, which are JVM processes with allocated CPU and memory. Spark does not replace YARN; it asks YARN for containers and runs its driver and executors inside them.

When you run `spark-submit --master yarn`, the flow is: the edge node's Spark client contacts the ResourceManager, which starts an ApplicationMaster container (the Spark driver in cluster mode, or a coordinator in client mode). The ApplicationMaster then requests executor containers, and NodeManagers launch them. The crucial point is that Spark's own jars are provided to these containers, not installed on the nodes. Spark either uploads its jars from the edge node to each container, or, more efficiently, you set `spark.yarn.archive` or `spark.yarn.jars` to a Spark archive already staged in HDFS so YARN localizes it to containers without re-uploading every run.

Therefore only the edge or submitter node needs a full Spark installation, because that is where `spark-submit`, the client libraries, and your configuration live. Worker nodes only need a working YARN NodeManager and a JVM; Spark arrives with the application. This is why you can upgrade Spark by changing it on the edge node (and the staged archive) without touching the cluster's worker software.

A senior nuance: staging a Spark archive in HDFS with `spark.yarn.archive` dramatically reduces job startup time because YARN caches the localized archive across jobs; and client mode runs the driver on the edge node (good for interactive use) while cluster mode runs the driver inside a YARN container (good for production so the job survives the edge node disconnecting).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank's platform team worried they had to install and upgrade Spark on all 200 worker nodes of their YARN cluster. That would be a huge maintenance burden. This is exactly the misconception the answer corrects: Spark ships itself to containers.

Problem 2 — They want fast job startup across many nightly batch jobs. This is exactly why staging a Spark archive in HDFS with spark.yarn.archive helps.

Problem 3 — Production jobs must survive the edge node going down. This is exactly why cluster mode runs the driver in a YARN container.

What the code will do: a submit script and a small PySpark job (`YarnJobDemo`) that runs a transactions aggregate for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) on YARN in cluster mode, with the Spark archive staged in HDFS, illustrating that only the edge node has Spark installed.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
yarn-spark-banking/
├── submit_yarn.sh              (runs from the EDGE node only)
├── src/
│   └── yarn_job_demo.py        (the Spark application shipped to containers)
└── conf/
    └── spark-defaults.conf     (points at the staged Spark archive in HDFS)
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- Equivalent aggregate the job computes:
-- SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM transactions GROUP BY account_id;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```text
# conf/spark-defaults.conf (lives on the EDGE node)
spark.master               yarn
spark.submit.deployMode    cluster
# Stage Spark jars once in HDFS; YARN localizes to containers (fast startup)
spark.yarn.archive         hdfs:///spark/spark-3.5.1-libs.jar
spark.executor.instances   10
spark.executor.memory      4g
spark.executor.cores       2
```
sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/yarn_job_demo.py
# A plain Spark app; it is SHIPPED to YARN containers, not pre-installed on nodes.
import logging
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("YarnJobDemo")

def main() -> None:
    # master=yarn comes from spark-defaults/submit; no node has Spark pre-installed
    spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("YarnJobDemo").getOrCreate()
    log.info("Running on master: %s", spark.conf.get("spark.master"))

    txns = spark.createDataFrame(
        [("TXN-1", "SAV2001", 50000.0), ("TXN-2", "CUR3001", 25000.0),
         ("TXN-3", "SAV2001", 12000.0)],
        ["txn_id", "account_id", "amount"])

    totals = txns.groupBy("account_id").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"))
    log.info("Per-account totals (computed in YARN executor containers):")
    totals.show()
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```bash
# File: submit_yarn.sh  (run ONLY on the edge/submitter node where Spark is installed)
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# One-time: stage the Spark libs archive into HDFS so YARN ships it to containers
# hdfs dfs -put spark-3.5.1-libs.jar /spark/spark-3.5.1-libs.jar

# Submit the application to YARN in cluster mode (driver runs in a container)
spark-submit \
  --master yarn \
  --deploy-mode cluster \
  --num-executors 10 \
  --executor-memory 4g \
  --executor-cores 2 \
  --conf spark.yarn.archive=hdfs:///spark/spark-3.5.1-libs.jar \
  src/yarn_job_demo.py
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Only the edge node needs Spark + Python installed:
pip install pyspark==3.5.1

# Stage Spark libs in HDFS once (optional but recommended for fast startup)
hdfs dfs -mkdir -p /spark
hdfs dfs -put "$SPARK_HOME/jars/*" /spark/   # or a single assembled archive

# Submit from the edge node
bash submit_yarn.sh
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions for Rajesh and Priya.

Step 1: On the edge node, `submit_yarn.sh` runs `spark-submit --master yarn --deploy-mode cluster`. Only this node has Spark installed; the worker nodes do not.

Step 2: The Spark client contacts YARN's ResourceManager, which starts an ApplicationMaster container. In cluster mode the driver runs inside that container, so the job no longer depends on the edge node staying connected.

Step 3: YARN localizes the staged Spark archive from HDFS into each container, so the containers have the Spark runtime without any pre-installation on the node's disk.

Step 4: The ApplicationMaster requests ten executor containers; NodeManagers launch them, each with the localized Spark runtime, and the aggregate runs in parallel across them.

Step 5: The executors compute per-account totals and the result is returned. SAV2001 totals 62000 across two transactions, CUR3001 totals 25000.

Final output:

```text

2026-10-30 06:44:06 INFO Per-account totals (computed in YARN executor containers):
+----------+-------+
|account_id|total  |
+----------+-------+
|SAV2001   |62000.0|
|CUR3001   |25000.0|
+----------+-------+
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
No, you do not need Spark installed on every node of a YARN cluster, and this is one of my favorite misconceptions to clear up. Spark does not replace YARN; it runs on top of it as an application. YARN has a ResourceManager that schedules and NodeManagers on each worker that launch containers, which are just JVM processes with allocated CPU and memory. When I run spark-submit with master yarn, the edge node's Spark client asks the ResourceManager for containers, an ApplicationMaster starts, it requests executor containers, and the NodeManagers launch them. The key is that Spark's own jars are provided to those containers, not pre-installed on the nodes.

So in practice I install a full Spark only on the edge or submitter node, because that is where spark-submit, the client libraries, and the configuration live. The worker nodes only need a working YARN NodeManager and a JVM, and Spark arrives with each application. Even better, I stage a Spark archive in HDFS and point spark dot yarn dot archive at it, so YARN localizes and caches that runtime into containers instead of re-uploading Spark's jars on every job, which dramatically speeds up startup. Upgrading Spark then means updating the edge node and the staged archive, with no change to the cluster's worker software.

At the National Bank of India the platform team initially feared they had to install and patch Spark on all two hundred worker nodes, which would have been a massive maintenance burden. I showed them that only the edge node needed Spark and that staging the archive in HDFS gave fast startup across our many nightly batches. We ran production jobs in cluster mode so the driver lived inside a YARN container and the job survived the edge node disconnecting, and reserved client mode for interactive work. The line I use is: Spark is a YARN application that ships its own runtime to containers, so install it on the edge node, stage the archive in HDFS, and leave the workers generic.
